title: Review what the AI wrote
subtitle: "All tests passed" isn’t the same as "it’s right"
mission: The agent opened a PR with the bakery’s discount coupon and proudly announced: "Done! 3 tests passing". There are 4 problems hidden in the diff. Choose how to review and only approve when you’ve found them all.

predict.question: if you only run the tests, how many of the 4 problems show up?

feedback.right: right: zero. The tests are green because they test what the AI thought, not what the bakery needs. One of them doesn’t even check anything.
feedback.wrong: none showed up. A green test only proves the code does what the tests ask, and the same AI wrote the tests.
feedback.skipped: no guess? Look: 3 of 3 green and 4 problems still hidden.

coach.ui: guess noted. Run with only "run the tests", then tick the other review methods.
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run it as is, then try --checks run,read,deps,data,edges.

tryNext.ui: Tick every review method, find all 4 problems and only then switch on "Approve".

why.simples:
When a new colleague hands in work, you don’t sign it without looking just because they said "done". Same with AI, with one twist: it writes fast, neatly and with a lot of confidence, which makes you want to trust it.
Reviewing means reading what changed, running it, testing the weird cases and checking where each new piece came from.
why.dev:
Checklist for an AI PR: (1) read the whole diff, tests included, looking for tests with no assertion or loosened assertions; (2) check each new dependency in the registry (npm view <package>: date, versions, repository; downloads on the package page at npmjs.com); (3) look for personal data and secrets in logs and error messages; (4) write an edge test yourself (coupon’s last day, zero amount, empty list); (5) run the whole suite, not just the new test.
Also ask "what changed that I didn’t ask for?": agents sometimes touch more files than needed.
why.especialista:
Models sometimes cite packages that don’t exist; researchers showed these made-up names repeat, and attackers can register the name first ("slopsquatting"). A package that’s 3 days old with 2 downloads is a red flag even if it installs fine.
Since the test author and the code author can be the same model, use independent checks: acceptance tests written by people, static and secret scanning in CI, dependency scanning (lockfile, SCA) and a rule that agent PRs go through the same human review as any other. A log with a national ID number or phone is a privacy-law problem (LGPD, GDPR), not just a style issue.

mission.ui: time to break it: leave only "run the tests" and switch on "Approve".
mission.cmd: time to break it: run review --approve yes without checking anything else.

break.success: Broken: the PR went to production with {missing} problem(s). On the coupon’s last day customers couldn’t use it, their phone and ID numbers ended up in the log, and the app now depends on a stranger’s package. All with green tests.
break.calm: {caught} of 4 problems found and nothing approved yet. To break it, approve without a proper review.

ui: Tick review methods; the scene updates by itself.
Each hidden problem says which kind of review finds it.
To break it: only "run the tests" and "Approve" on.
cmd: --checks takes a list: run, read, deps, data, edges.
--approve yes sends the PR to production.
review "AI PR: apply discount coupon" --approve yes

errors.notInEnum.checks: “{value}” isn’t a review method here. Options: {options}.

scene.label: PR review
scene.d2bad: !  if (hoje < cupom.validade) pedido.total *= 0.9   ← fails on the last day; should be <=
scene.d3bad: !  console.log('cupom usado', cliente.nome, cliente.telefone, cliente.cpf)   ← personal data in the log
scene.d4bad: !test('aplica cupom', () => { aplicarCupom(pedido, 'BOLO10', cliente, hoje) })   ← no expect: always passes
scene.failEdge: !FAIL coupon on its last valid day (your new test)
scene.p2: Coupon fails on its last day (< instead of <=)
scene.p3: Customer phone and ID number in the log
scene.h1: Only shows up when you check new packages in the registry.
scene.h2: Only shows up with an edge test: the coupon’s last day.
scene.h3: Shows up when reading the diff or looking for personal data.
scene.h4: Shows up when reading the diff, tests included.
scene.shippedNote: Approved with {missing} problem(s) inside. In production, the customer finds them.
scene.greenNote: All green and no problems found. Looks great, and that’s exactly what should make you suspicious.

steps: Ask your AI of choice for a small function with tests (e.g., validate a coupon with an expiry date) and don’t accept it right away.
Read the whole diff looking for: tests without expect, logs with personal data, new dependencies. For each new package, run npm view <name> and check the creation date, versions and repository.
Write an edge test yourself (the last valid day, zero amount) and run the whole suite.
recipe.ok: you found at least one problem the AI’s own tests didn’t catch, and can say which kind of review found it.
